title: Feedback that changes behaviour, not just feelings

narration: I've said this line more than once.
"You need to be more proactive."
It changed nothing.
beats.visual_intent: The presenter to camera, a little rueful; the line appears beside her as a speech bubble

grounding.claim: a verdict about the person often changes nothing in what they do next

narration: Say your teammate Leo messages you on Thursday.
The report due today will be late.
You tell him to be more proactive.
He nods, and feels bad.
beats.visual_intent: Leo at his desk sends a message; a desk calendar shows Thursday circled as the due day; you reply with the verdict; Leo's face drops

grounding.claim: an invented, ordinary late deliverable used as the running example

narration: Two weeks later. Thursday again.
Same message. Same surprise.
beats.visual_intent: The calendar pages flip forward two weeks to another Thursday; the same late message pops up on the same screen

grounding.claim: vague feedback does not specify which action to repeat or stop, so the same thing tends to happen again

narration: His feelings changed. His actions didn't.
Let's fix that one sentence.
beats.visual_intent: Two dials beside Leo: a feelings dial that has swung down, an actions dial that has not moved at all

grounding.claim: person-directed or vague feedback tends to change how someone feels, not what they do next
vague feedback gives no action to repeat or change

narration: "Proactive" is a label about Leo,
not something he did.
And labels tend to make people defensive.
beats.visual_intent: The word 'proactive' detaches from the bubble and sticks on Leo like a name tag; Leo folds his arms

grounding.claim: a trait framing labels the person's character, a behaviour framing describes one observable action
feedback aimed at a trait tends to trigger defensiveness

narration: It doesn't say what to change, either.
Which action should he fix?
beats.visual_intent: Above Leo, a cloud of possible actions, each with a question mark; none is picked out

grounding.claim: vague feedback does not specify which action to repeat or stop, so even a person who wants to improve does not know what to change

beats.misconception: if I say the problem clearly and firmly, the person will do it differently next time

narration: So start with what you saw.
"You told me on Thursday, the due day."
An action, not a character.
beats.visual_intent: The name tag peels off Leo; in its place the first of three marks appears: what he did, with Thursday marked on the calendar

grounding.claim: effective feedback names a specific, observed behaviour at a particular time rather than a trait
a specific behaviour gives a concrete unit of action instead of a label

narration: Next, the impact.
"I had to move the client call at short notice."
beats.visual_intent: The second mark joins the first: a meeting card on the calendar slides from Thursday to the following week

grounding.claim: effective feedback states the concrete impact of the behaviour, such as an effect on a deadline

narration: Then stop telling, and ask.
"What would help you flag a slip sooner?"
beats.visual_intent: The third mark joins the row; your speech bubble turns into a question bubble pointed at Leo, who looks up

grounding.claim: effective feedback ends with a question that invites the other person's view, turning a verdict into a conversation

narration: Leo knows his week better than you.
Say he suggests a midpoint check-in.
You agree it together.
beats.visual_intent: Leo answers; a small check-in pin lands on Tuesday, the midpoint of the calendar, and both of them nod

grounding.claim: the conversation closes with an agreed next step so both know what will change

narration: What he did. What it caused.
Then a question, and one next step you agree.
on_screen: Ask, then agree a next step
beats.visual_intent: The three marks hold as one row, each lighting as it is named

grounding.claim: behaviour, impact, a question and an agreed next step, in that order
impact
question
next step

narration: Quick check. Two lines.
A: "Be more proactive."
B: "You told me on the due day,
and I had to move the client call.
What would help you flag it sooner?"
Which one gives Leo something to do?
on_screen: B: due day, call moved, what would help?
beats.visual_intent: The two lines side by side as two cards the viewer can compare; a short pause before the answer

recall.prompt: Which one gives Leo something to do?

grounding.claim: the two lines are invented examples of a trait verdict and the behaviour, impact, question shape

narration: B.
A feels honest, and Leo reacts.
But reacting isn't knowing what to change.
B gives him an action.
beats.visual_intent: Card B is marked as the answer and splits into its three marks; card A dims

recall.why_wrong_tempting: A feels direct and Leo reacts at once, but reacting is not knowing what to change

grounding.claim: vague feedback names no action to repeat or stop
naming behaviour and impact gives a concrete unit of action

narration: Back to Leo. Two weeks on.
Tuesday, the midpoint, his message comes early.
There's time to fix it.
beats.visual_intent: The opening desk and calendar again; this time the message arrives on Tuesday at the check-in pin, and you both have time to rearrange

grounding.claim: an agreed next step means both know what will change going forward

narration: Next time you want someone to be more something,
name what they did, what it caused,
and ask what would help.
on_screen: What they did. What it caused. Ask.
beats.visual_intent: The presenter to camera to close, the three marks beside her

grounding.claim: behaviour, impact, then a question
impact
question
